en: The Section on the Suspension of the Poṣadha; the summary verse for the section on the suspension of the Poṣadha:
"Because of an impure Poṣadha, the monk was caused to be expelled by Maudgalyāyana."
Then, having censured the treatises, the Poṣadha was questioned by the Saṃgha.
This summary verse is found in detail in the Poṣadha-sūtra at Campā;
and that Poṣadha-sūtra is recited in the Saṃgīti-nipāta of the Madhyama Āgama.
The summary verse: Reprimand and reminder, granting leave and the state of being beyond reproach, instruction, sending away, the *poṣadha*, and the *pravāraṇā*.
The Blessed One has said that the recitation of the Prātimokṣa-sūtra must be performed every half-month by the Elder of the Saṃgha.
Therefore, the steward, standing before the Elder of the Saṃgha, says:
"Elder, please recite the Prātimokṣa-sūtra."
He said,
"Venerable sir,
the assembly of monks is indeed pure."
"Who has been seen by the Elder here as being impure?
You yourself, first of all.
How have you been seen by the Elder?"
"With the divine eye!
Alas, we are now lost,
since monks, having seen with the divine eye, would exhort and remind us."
The monks reported this matter to the Blessed One.
The Blessed One said:
"Monks, the divine eye is not to be used for worldly transaction."
Therefore, a monk must not, having seen with the divine eye, reprove or remind another monk.
If a monk, having seen with the divine eye, reproves or reminds another monk, he commits an offense of transgression (*sātisāra*).
As it is with the divine eye, so it is with the divine ear.
Again, that superintendent of the monastery stood before the elder of the Saṃgha and said,
"Elder, please recite the Prātimokṣa Sūtra.
He replied:
"Venerable sir, the assembly of monks is not yet pure.
"Elder, who here is impure?
"You yourself, first of all."
"Elder, how is it that you have struck me on the head with your fist in the midst of the Saṅgha? Oh, how I wish I had been admonished by you in private!
He, however, remained silent.
The monks reported this matter to the Blessed One.
The Blessed One said:
"He should be reproved in private, not in the midst of the Saṃgha."
If, when questioned in private, he does not remember, he should be reminded;
if, having been reminded, he becomes angry, he should be given an opportunity [to respond].
When one who is being made to stand in the *avakāśa* position resorts to another person instead of the one [he should address],
the Blessed One said:
"He should be made subject to the *avacanīya* (reproach) procedure."
He was made subject to censure;
nevertheless, he evaded one point with another.
The Blessed One said:
Instruction should be given to him regarding the suspension of the *poṣadha* and the *pravāraṇā*.
There is one suspension of the *poṣadha* that is non-dharmic and one that is dharmic;
two that are non-dharmic and two that are dharmic.
Three are unrighteous, three are righteous;
four are unrighteous, four are righteous;
five are unrighteous, five are righteous.
Six are unrighteous and six are righteous; seven are unrighteous and seven are righteous;
eight are unrighteous and eight are righteous.

There are nine unrighteous and nine righteous ways of suspending the *poṣadha*; there are ten unrighteous and ten righteous ways of suspending the *poṣadha*. There is one unrighteous way of suspending the *poṣadha* and one righteous way.
What is unrighteous?
To suspend the *poṣadha* on account of a groundless charge is an unrighteous suspension of the *poṣadha*. What is a righteous suspension of the *poṣadha*?

One suspends the *poṣadha* on account of a transgression committed together with its root; this is a lawful suspension of the *poṣadha*. This is one unlawful suspension of the *poṣadha* and one lawful suspension.
There are two ways of suspending the *poṣadha* that are contrary to the Dharma, and two that are in accordance with the Dharma.
Which are they?
One suspends the *poṣadha* on the basis of groundless non-action and groundless action; this is the suspension of the *poṣadha* that is contrary to the Dharma.
One suspends the *poṣadha* on account of something uncommitted with its root, or on account of something committed with its root; this is a lawful suspension of the *poṣadha*.
These two are unlawful suspensions of the *poṣadha*, and these two are lawful. There are three unlawful suspensions of the *poṣadha* and three lawful suspensions of the *poṣadha*.
Which are they?

When one suspends the *poṣadha* on account of a groundless charge for what has been done, a groundless charge for what has not been done, or a groundless charge for both what has been done and what has not been done, that suspension of the *poṣadha* is contrary to the Dharma. When one suspends the *poṣadha* on account of a grounded charge for what has been done, a grounded charge for what has not been done, or a grounded charge for both what has been done and what has not been done, that suspension of the *poṣadha* is in accordance with the Dharma.
These three are unlawful suspensions of the *poṣadha*; these three are lawful.
There are four unlawful suspensions of the *poṣadha* and four lawful ones.
Which are they?

If one suspends the *poṣadha* on account of a groundless failure in morality, a failure in view, a failure in conduct, or a failure in livelihood, that suspension of the *poṣadha* is contrary to the Dharma (*adhārmika*).

If one suspends the *poṣadha* on account of a grounded failure in morality, a failure in view, a failure in conduct, or a failure in livelihood, that suspension of the *poṣadha* is in accordance with the Dharma (*dhārmika*).
These are the four suspensions of the *poṣadha* that are contrary to the Dharma and the four that are in accordance with the Dharma.
There are five unrighteous and five righteous ways of suspending the *poṣadha*.
What are they?

One suspends the *poṣadha* on the basis of a groundless charge of a *pārājika*, a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*, a *pāyantika*, a *pratideśanīya*, or a *duṣkṛta*; this is the unrighteous suspension of the *poṣadha*.

(MSV III 110) One suspends the *poṣadha* by means of an offense involving roots, a *pārājika*, a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*, a *pāyantika*, a *pratideśanīya*, or a *duṣkṛta*; this is a legitimate suspension of the *poṣadha*.
These are the five illegitimate suspensions of the *poṣadha* and the five legitimate ones.
There are six illegitimate suspensions of the *poṣadha* and six legitimate suspensions of the *poṣadha*.
Which are they?

By means of groundless [accusations] regarding what was done, by means of groundless [accusations] regarding what was not done, and by means of groundless [accusations] regarding both what was done and what was not done; and by means of groundless [accusations] regarding what was done with remainder, by means of groundless [accusations] regarding what was not done with remainder, and by means of groundless [accusations] regarding both what was done and what was not done with remainder—one suspends the *poṣadha*. This is an unrighteous suspension of the *poṣadha*.

By means of a complete [charge] regarding what was done, a complete [charge] regarding what was not done, and a complete [charge] regarding both what was done and what was not done; by means of a complete [charge] regarding what was done with remainder, a complete [charge] regarding what was not done with remainder, and a complete [charge] regarding both what was done and what was not done with remainder—one suspends the *poṣadha*. This is the lawful suspension of the *poṣadha*.
These six are unlawful suspensions of the *poṣadha*, and these six are lawful.
There are seven unrighteous ways of suspending the *poṣadha*, and seven righteous ways of suspending the *poṣadha*.
Which are they?

One suspends the *poṣadha* on account of a groundless failure in morality, a failure in view, a failure in conduct, or a failure in livelihood; or on account of what has been seen, heard, or suspected without foundation—this is an unrighteous suspension of the *poṣadha*.

By means of a downfall in morality, a downfall in view, a downfall in conduct, or a downfall in livelihood, together with their roots; and by means of what has been seen, heard, or suspected together with its root—one suspends the *poṣadha*.
These are the seven unlawful and the seven lawful ways of suspending the *poṣadha*. There are eight unlawful and eight lawful ways of suspending the *poṣadha*.
Which are they?
By means of groundless charges of a *pārājika*, a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*, a *pāyantika*, a *pratideśanīya*, or a *duṣkṛta*;
or by means of groundless [charges] based on what has been seen, heard, or suspected—one suspends the *poṣadha*. This is an unrighteous suspension of the *poṣadha*.

If one suspends the *poṣadha* on account of a *pārājika* offense together with its root, a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*, a *pāyantika*, a *pratideśanīya*, or a *duṣkṛta*— or on account of what has been seen, heard, or suspected together with its root— it is a lawful suspension of the *poṣadha*. These are the eight unlawful suspensions of the *poṣadha* and the eight lawful ones.
There are nine unrighteous and nine righteous ways of suspending the *poṣadha*.
Which are they?
[They are] by means of groundless charges for what has been done, for what has not been done, and for what has both been done and not been done.

If one suspends the *poṣadha* on the basis of groundless charges that are partially accomplished, groundless charges that are unaccomplished, or groundless charges that are both accomplished and unaccomplished; or on the basis of groundless charges that are fully accomplished, groundless charges that are unaccomplished, or groundless charges that are both accomplished and unaccomplished—this is an illegal suspension of the *poṣadha*.
[Likewise for] charges that are well-founded whether they are accomplished, unaccomplished, or both accomplished and unaccomplished.

If one suspends the Poṣadha on account of a transgression that is accompanied by its root, with a remainder; or on account of a transgression that is accompanied by its root, without a remainder; or on account of a transgression that is accompanied by its root, both committed and uncommitted, with a remainder; or on account of a transgression that is accompanied by its root, committed without a remainder; or on account of a transgression that is accompanied by its root, uncommitted without a remainder; or on account of a transgression that is accompanied by its root, both committed and uncommitted, without a remainder—this is the lawful suspension of the Poṣadha.
These nine are unrighteous ways of suspending the *poṣadha*, while these nine are righteous.
There are ten unrighteous and ten righteous ways of suspending the *poṣadha*.
Which are they?
He does not become one who has committed a *pārājika* offense;
the discourse on the *pārājika* offenses has not been violated;
and the training has not been renounced.
The discourse on the renunciation of the training is not disregarded,
nor is the Saṃgha rejected.
The discourse on the rejection of the Saṅgha has not been violated;
he is not one who has failed in morality, nor failed in view, nor failed in conduct, nor failed in livelihood.
How is it that he does not become one who has committed a pārājika offense?
If a monk sees neither the forms, nor the signs, nor the marks by which one commits an offense involving defeat (pārājika),
and yet, without having seen, heard, or suspected it, he suspends the *poṣadha* ceremony; [he is at fault].
The suspension of the *poṣadha* is unrighteous;
thus, one does not become one who has committed a *pārājika* offense.
How, then, is the discussion of a *pārājika* offense not interrupted?
It is just as when a great number of monks are seated together in assembly,
and that conversation is neither shameful, nor centered on that [topic], nor interrupted;
yet those monks rise from their seats and depart in various directions.
If he establishes the suspension of the Poṣadha without having seen, heard, or suspected [the offense],
that establishment of the Poṣadha is contrary to the Dharma;
in this way, the discussion regarding a Pārājika offense remains unsettled.
How is it that the training is not renounced?

A monk does not see, through those modes, those characteristics, or those signs by which the renunciation of the training is performed, that [another] is performing the renunciation of the training through those modes, those characteristics, or those signs.
If he establishes the suspension of the *poṣadha* without having seen, heard, or suspected [an offense],
that is an unrighteous suspension of the *poṣadha*;
in this way, the training has not been renounced.
How is it that a discussion concerning the rejection of the training is not interrupted? It is when many monks are seated together in assembly,
and that discussion is neither shameful, nor absorbed in [other matters], nor interrupted.
And those monks, having risen from their seats, departed in various directions.
Without seeing them, without hearing from them, and without suspecting anything, he suspended the *poṣadha*;
this is an unrighteous suspension of the *poṣadha*.
In this way, the discourse on the rejection of the training is not violated.
How is it that the Saṃgha is not rejected?

By whatever modes, whatever characteristics, and whatever signs the Saṃgha is rejected, if that monk perceives them not by those modes, nor by those characteristics, nor by those signs, [then there is no rejection of the Saṃgha].
If one,
without having seen, heard, or suspected [the offense], suspends the *poṣadha*,
that suspension of the *poṣadha* is contrary to the Dharma.
In this way, the Saṃgha is not rejected.
How is it that the discourse on rejecting the Saṃgha does not become disrupted?
It is, for example, when many monks are seated together in an assembly.
And that talk was neither shameful, nor was it focused on that [topic], nor was it interrupted;
yet those monks, having risen from their seats, departed in various directions.
Without having seen, heard, or suspected anything [of the offense], he suspended the Poṣadha ceremony.
The suspension of the *poṣadha* is unrighteous;
thus, the discourse on the rejection of the Saṃgha is not violated.
How is it that one does not become fallen from morality?
If a monk has committed any one of the four *pārājika* offenses,
and another monk, without having seen, heard, or suspected it, suspends the *poṣadha*,
that suspension of the *poṣadha* is contrary to the Dharma.
In this way, one does not fail in ethical discipline.
How does one not fail in view?
One does not become attached to any one of the sixty-two types of views.
And if a monk, without having seen, heard, or suspected [an offense], suspends the Poṣadha,
that suspension of the Poṣadha is contrary to the Dharma;
thus, he does not become one who has fallen away from right view.
How does one not fail in conduct?
When being addressed with words that are conformable and conducive to training, one practices correctly.
If a monk, without having seen, heard, or suspected [an offense], suspends the Poṣadha,
that suspension of the Poṣadha is contrary to the Dharma;
in this way, he does not become one who has failed in conduct.
How does one not fail in livelihood?
His livelihood is completely pure,
yet a monk, without having seen, heard, or suspected it to be so, suspends his *poṣadha*.
The suspension of the *poṣadha* is unrighteous;
thus, one does not become fallen from right livelihood.
In the white category, one becomes one who has committed a *pārājika* offense.
The discourse on the *pārājika* offenses has been interrupted;
the training has been renounced;
and the discourse on the renunciation of the training has been interrupted.
The Saṅgha has been rejected;
the discourse concerning the rejection of the Saṅgha has been interrupted.
He is one who has failed in morality, failed in view, failed in conduct, and failed in livelihood.
How does one become one who has committed a *pārājika* offense?

By whatever modes, by whatever characteristics, and by whatever signs one incurs a *pārājika* offense—if a monk sees [another] not incurring a *pārājika* offense by those modes, those characteristics, and those signs; yet [he himself] does see [himself] incurring a *pārājika* offense by those modes, those characteristics, and those signs.
Having seen, heard, or suspected [an offense], he suspends the *poṣadha*;
this is a lawful suspension of the *poṣadha*,
and thus he does not become one who has committed a *pārājika* offense.
How is the discussion on the *pārājika* offenses interrupted?
It is when many monks are seated together in assembly, and that discussion becomes shameful; thus, being absorbed by it, the discussion is interrupted.
And while those monks were thus seated,
he— having seen, heard, and become suspicious— suspended the *poṣadha*.
This was a lawful suspension of the *poṣadha*.
In this way, the discussion regarding the *pārājika* offenses is interrupted.
How is the training (*śikṣā*) renounced?

When a monk perceives through those modes, those characteristics, and those signs by which the renunciation of the training is performed—that renunciation of the training [is established] through those modes, those characteristics, and those signs.
While he was doing so, the other, having seen it, heard it, and become suspicious, suspends the *poṣadha*;
this is a lawful suspension of the *poṣadha*.
In this way, the training is renounced.
How does a discourse on the renunciation of the training become interrupted?
It is as follows: many monks are seated together in an assembly.
That conversation becomes a cause for shame, and she has been offended by me;
while those monks remain seated in that very manner,
he— having seen, heard, and suspected— suspends the Poṣadha ceremony.
The suspension of the *poṣadha* for a righteous reason is thus a violation of the discourse on the renunciation of training. How, then, is the Saṃgha rejected?

If a monk sees that the Saṃgha is being rejected by certain modes, signs, and marks, and having seen and heard it, he becomes suspicious that they are performing the rejection of the Saṃgha through those very modes, signs, and marks, he shall suspend the Poṣadha.
The suspension of the *poṣadha* ceremony for one who is righteous [is invalid];
in this way, the Saṃgha is rejected.
How is the discourse regarding the rejection of the Saṃgha interrupted?
It is as when many monks are seated together in assembly,
and that conversation becomes shameful and is interrupted by them;
yet those monks remain seated exactly as they were.
Having seen, heard, or suspected [an offense], he suspends the *poṣadha*;
this is a lawful suspension of the *poṣadha*.
In this way, the discourse regarding the rejection of the Saṃgha becomes disturbed.
How does one fail in morality?
One has committed any one of the four *pārājika* offenses;
and having seen, heard, or suspected this, a monk suspends the *poṣadha* for him.
The suspension of the *poṣadha* is lawful.
In this way, one becomes fallen from morality.
How does one become fallen from view?
He becomes adhered to one or another of the sixty-two views.
Upon seeing or hearing of him, or suspecting it of him, the monk suspends the *poṣadha*;
this is a lawful suspension of the *poṣadha*.
In this way, one is corrupted in view.
How is one corrupted in conduct?
When being addressed with words that are conformable and conducive to the training, one does not practice correctly.
If a monk, having seen, heard, or suspected this, suspends the Poṣadha,
that suspension of the Poṣadha is lawful;
thus he is one who has failed in conduct.
How does one fail in livelihood? One's livelihood is impure; and having seen, heard, or suspected this, a monk suspends the *poṣadha* ceremony for him.
The suspension of the *poṣadha* is lawful.
In this way, one becomes corrupted in livelihood.
These are the ten unlawful and the ten lawful suspensions of the *poṣadha*.
Just as with the suspension of the *poṣadha*, so too is the suspension of the *pravāraṇā*.
Monks, there are these five Saṃghas.
Which five?
The shameless Saṃgha, the sheep-like and mute Saṃgha, the factional Saṃgha, the conventional Saṃgha, and the ultimate Saṃgha.
What is the shameless Saṃgha? It is where all the monks are of immoral conduct and possess evil qualities.
What is a community of the deaf and mute? It is one where there is no upholder of the Sūtras, no upholder of the Vinaya, and no upholder of the Mātṛkās.
What is a communal assembly (gaṇasaṃgha)?
Where rituals are performed in connection with a group, that is the conventional Saṃgha. Who are all those? All virtuous ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana-kalyāṇaka*).
What is the ultimate Saṃgha?
It consists of the eight persons of great worth who are both those in training (śaikṣa) and those beyond training (aśaikṣa).

Regarding this, as for the three previous types of Saṃgha—the shameless Saṃgha, the Saṃgha of the dumb and mute, and the Saṃgha of the assembly—it is permissible for them to perform legal acts (karman) that are contrary to the Dharma.
This conventional Saṅgha can be acted upon by one who perceives it as the Dharma through an illegal formal act;
however, this ultimate Saṅgha cannot be acted upon by one through an illegal formal act.
The section on the suspension of the Poṣadha ceremony is completed.
